# A small endpoint among three arbitrary convex fibers: compact boundary exclusion

For every fixed integer d>=2 there is rho_d>0 with the following
property. Let A,B,C be full-dimensional compact convex bodies in R^d,
with

    (A+C)/2 subset B,
    a=|A|>0, V=|B|>0, W=|C|>0, a/V<=rho_d.

Then the actual three-fiber mixed set

    S=({-1} times A) union ({0} times B) union ({1} times C)

has a point whose mass in every containing closed ambient halfspace
is at least

    (Gamma/2)(a+V+W),   Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d.           (1)

The large fibers need not be simplices or have equal volumes. The
constant rho_d is proved positive by a complete compactness argument;
no numerical or explicit rate is claimed. The proof constructs a
middle-fiber point near its TRUE ordinary centroid in the non-heavy
limiting regime. It does not identify that point with the true mixed
centroid, and does not classify or deform all extracted maximizers.

The convex hull of the three lifted fibers has exactly these integer
fibers. At the only intermediate integer base, its additional endpoint
contribution is (A+C)/2, already inside B. Thus this is a statement
about actual convex-compatible fibers and all ambient halfspaces.

## 1. Ordinary inputs and an elementary bounded normalization

We use the independently proved ordinary theorem
`candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`:

    D(K)>=Gamma, with equality exactly for simplices,         (2)

where D(K) is the maximum ordinary normalized halfspace depth. Its
proof uses classical Grunbaum with its single-cap equality case.
The same note proves that D is continuous under total-variation
convergence of normalized uniform measures. Hausdorff convergence to
a full-dimensional convex body implies that total-variation convergence.

For bounded normalization, choose a maximum-volume inscribed simplex
of B and send it by a continuous affine map to

    T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), v=|T|=1/d!.

The maximum exists by compactness of the (d+1)-fold vertex parameter
space and continuity of determinant. It has positive volume. Write
lambda_0,...,lambda_d for the barycentric coordinate functions of T.
Replacing its i-th vertex by any x in B produces a simplex of volume
|lambda_i(x)|v, so maximality gives |lambda_i(x)|<=1. Consequently

    T subset B subset [-1,1]^d.                    (3)

In particular v<=V<=2^d. This normalization uses no transformation
of the integer coordinate.

Next choose p_0 in A and shear (z,x) to (z,x+z p_0). Renaming the
fibers, 0 belongs to A, C subset 2B, and A subset 2(B-B). Therefore

    A subset [-4,4]^d, C subset [-2,2]^d.           (4)

All continuous affine maps and these shears preserve the mixed lattice,
all halfspaces, and all relative masses. We can use the single bound
R=4 sqrt(d) on A union B union C throughout the normalized proof.

## 2. A failure sequence has two simplex limits

Suppose the theorem were false. There would be a sequence of failing
triples with a_k/V_k tending to zero. If either V_k>=W_k+a_k or
W_k>=V_k+a_k, that fiber alone has mass at least half the total.
Its ordinary centroid and Grunbaum give (1) immediately. Thus failure
forces

    |W_k-V_k|<a_k,       W_k/V_k ->1.               (5)

For any point in any one fiber, its mixed halfspace depth is at least
its ordinary absolute depth in that fiber: every ambient containing
cap has a containing trace there and only adds nonnegative other mass.
In particular failure implies

    Gamma<=D(B_k)<=Gamma(a_k+V_k+W_k)/(2V_k),
    Gamma<=D(C_k)<=Gamma(a_k+V_k+W_k)/(2W_k).

Both right sides tend to Gamma. Apply (3)--(4) separately to each triple.
Blaschke selection yields a common subsequence with Hausdorff limits
B_* and C_*. The former contains T; the latter has volume
lim W_k=lim V_k>=v>0. Both are full dimensional. Volume and normalized
uniform measures converge. By (2), both limits are simplices.

In fact B_*=T. Every inscribed simplex of each normalized B_k has
volume at most v. Approximate the d+1 vertices of the simplex B_*
by points in B_k; the resulting simplex volumes converge to |B_*|.
Hence |B_*|<=v. Since T subset B_*, equality of volumes forces B_*=T.
We have obtained

    B_k -> T, C_k -> C_* a simplex,
    V_k,W_k ->v, a_k ->0, g_k:=centroid(B_k)->g:=centroid(T). (6)

No rate relating the Hausdorff error to a_k is asserted. In particular
an error o(a_k) is NOT required in what follows.

## 3. An approximate simplex still supplies fixed endpoint credits

Put N=d+1, b=1/N, J=ceil(N/2), L=N-J+1, and

    delta_0=N^(-N/(2L))-1/N>0,
    delta=delta_0/2>0.                              (7)

Choose inscribed simplices S_k subset C_k by approximating the vertices
of C_*. Then |S_k|->v. There are numbers e_k>=0 tending to zero for
which

    B_k subset T_k^+=(1+e_k)(T-g)+g.                (8)

For example, if g+rB_d subset T and the Hausdorff error is h_k,
the support inequalities give (8) with e_k=h_k/r. Discard finitely
many terms so e_k<=1/2.

For every p in A_k, the simplex (p+S_k)/2 lies in B_k and hence T_k^+.
Its nonnegative column-stochastic barycentric matrix P has determinant

    |det P|=2^-d |S_k|/|T_k^+| ->2^-d,             (9)

uniformly in p; its volume does not depend on the translation p.
The centered-row Hadamard proof in
`candidate 986ab1688d049a3b`
gives, for decreasing row maxima p_1>=...>=p_N,

    |det P|<=N^(N/2) 2^(-(N-1)) product_(i=2)^N p_i
             <=N^(N/2) 2^(-(N-1)) p_J^L.

Thus (9) implies p_J>=b+delta for all large k, uniformly in p.
For an explicit sufficient determinant threshold, it is enough that

    |S_k|/|T_k^+| >= [(b+delta)/(b+delta_0)]^L <1.

The barycentric coordinates of T_k^+ obey
lambda_i^+(x)=b+(lambda_i(x)-b)/(1+e_k). Therefore the row-max bound
implies, at each p, at least J indices with

    lambda_i(p)+h_{k,i}>=2b+2delta,
    h_{k,i}=max_(C_k) lambda_i.                    (10)

We used h_(C_k)>=h_(S_k) and e_k>=0. Define FIXED sets and credits

    A_{k,i}={p in A_k:lambda_i(p)+h_{k,i}>=2b+delta},
    c_{k,i}=|A_{k,i}|, cbar_k=N^(-1) sum_i c_{k,i}.

Then

    0<=c_{k,i}<=a_k,       cbar_k>=J a_k/N.          (11)

The chosen high-coordinate indices may vary with p. Equation (11)
comes from integrating their actual indicators. No diameter shrinkage
or fixed-shape assumption on A_k is used.

For any fixed p in A_k, (p+C_k)/2 subset B_k subset T_k^+ also gives

    width_(C_k)(lambda_i)<=2(1+e_k)<=3.             (12)

## 4. Uniform endpoint credit for nearby directions and centers

For brevity omit k in this section. Set r_A=(a/W)^(1/d), which tends
to zero along (6). Consider f_i(x)=lambda_i(x)+e.x, with |e|<=epsilon
and nonzero gradient, and a point y satisfying

    max_i(lambda_i(y)-b)_+<=sigma.

For EVERY integer tilt beta, the endpoint cap sum obeys

    |A intersect {f_i>=f_i(y)+beta}|
      +|C intersect {f_i>=f_i(y)-beta}|
       >= |A intersect {f_i>=2f_i(y)-h_C(f_i)
                                  +width_C(f_i) r_A}|.       (13)

For all sufficiently large k, r_A<=1. A copy of C homothetic toward
an f_i-maximizer with ratio r_A has volume a and lies in the cap at
h_C(f_i)-width_C(f_i)r_A. If the actual C cap has at least that mass,
it pays the right side of (13). Otherwise its threshold is strictly
larger, forcing the A threshold strictly below the right-side threshold.
This proves (13) for all tilts; no extremizing tilt or compactness of
tilt parameters is needed.

For p in A_i put q=R epsilon. By (4), (12), and the definition of A_i,

    f_i(p)+h_C(f_i)>=2b+delta-2q,
    f_i(y)<=b+sigma+q, width_C(f_i)<=3+2q.

Consequently the signed margin in (13) is at least

    delta-2sigma-3r_A-4q-2q r_A
       >=delta-2sigma-3r_A-6R epsilon.              (14)

In particular, if

    sigma<=delta/8, r_A<=delta/12,
    epsilon<=delta/(24R),                           (15)

then (14) is at least delta/4>0. The actual endpoint sum is therefore
at least the SAME fixed c_i for every allowed y, normal perturbation,
and real tilt.

## 5. Uniform convergence of proper section densities

We record the needed elementary continuity statement to justify the
middle-fiber derivative comparison. If K_l converge to a full-dimensional
K in Hausdorff distance, nonzero normals u_l converge to u, and levels
s_l converge to s strictly between min_K u.x and max_K u.x, then

    H_(d-1)(K_l intersect {u_l.x=s_l})/|u_l|
      -> H_(d-1)(K intersect {u.x=s})/|u|.           (16)

Identify the moving hyperplanes with the limiting one by isometries
and translations tending to the identity. Any limit point of the
sections belongs to the limiting section. Conversely the limiting
section contains a point of int K. Interpolating any section point
toward it gives an interior section point, and small adjustments to
the moving plane stay inside K_l for all large l. This approximates
the whole limiting section and proves Hausdorff convergence. Convex
(d-1)-volume is continuous under that convergence. For d=1 the proper
sections are singleton points of H_0 mass one. Division by the nonzero
normal is continuous. This proves (16) without boundary smoothness.

The assertion is uniform on a compact collection of limiting proper
planes: otherwise a sequence of violating planes has a convergent
subsequence, contradicting (16). We apply it to B_k->T, levels near
the TRUE centroid of B_k, and normals near a fixed facet direction.

Write n_i=grad lambda_i. For the exact simplex T, the cap
lambda_i>=s has volume v(1-s)^d for 0<s<1. At s=b its coarea density is

    d v(1-b)^(d-1)=N Gamma v.                       (17)

Continuity (16) and (17) have the following precise consequence. For
every zeta>0 one can choose epsilon>0 and h>0, depending only on T
and zeta, such that for all sufficiently large k, all i, |e|<=epsilon,
and |t|<=h,

    | S_(B_k)(lambda_i+e.x,
                    (lambda_i+e.x)(g_k)+t)-N Gamma V_k |
        <=zeta V_k,                                (18)

where S is section measure divided by the functional's gradient norm.
All these planes are proper. First choose epsilon,h small enough on
the fixed simplex, then use compact uniformity in (16), g_k->g and
V_k->v. Thus the error in (18) can be made a fixed arbitrarily small
constant; it need not be o(a_k).

## 6. One translated true centroid and every near-facet cap

Define

    kappa_d=J/N-Gamma>0, eta=kappa_d/2,
    K_d=sqrt(d)/(N Gamma).

Positivity uses d>=2, since J/N>=1/2>Gamma. Let v_k in R^d be the
unique translation with

    n_i.v_k=(c_{k,i}-cbar_k)/(N Gamma V_k)
                       for all i=0,...,d,
    y_k=g_k+v_k.                                   (19)

Existence follows because the prescribed right sides sum to zero
and the barycentric gradients have the sole dependence sum n_i=0.
In standard coordinates the components of v_k are the right sides
for i=1,...,d. Hence

    |v_k|<=K_d a_k/V_k.                            (20)

For all sufficiently large k, y_k is inside T and hence inside B_k,
and its upward barycentric deviation sigma satisfies (15).

Choose zeta and epsilon in (18) small enough also to satisfy

    zeta K_d(sqrt(d)+1)<=eta/2,
    epsilon<=min{1,delta/(24R),eta/(2 sqrt(d))}.     (21)

For f=lambda_i+e.x with |e|<=epsilon, put

    Delta_(k,f)=f(y_k)-f(g_k)=(n_i+e).v_k.

This is the linear translation increment, not evaluation of the affine
functional at v_k. Equation (20) gives |Delta_(k,f)|<=h for all large
k. The exact coarea integral, with its signed orientation if this
increment is negative, and (18) show

    | integral_0^(Delta_(k,f)) S_(B_k)(f,f(g_k)+t)dt
                    -N Gamma V_k n_i.v_k |
       <=zeta V_k |Delta_(k,f)|+N Gamma V_k |e.v_k|
       <=eta a_k.                                 (22)

Here |grad f|<=sqrt(d)+1 and N Gamma K_d=sqrt(d) were used.
Grunbaum at the TRUE ordinary centroid g_k gives its initial cap mass
at least Gamma V_k for every f. Equations (19)--(22) therefore imply

    |B_k intersect {f>=f(y_k)}|
        >=Gamma V_k-(c_{k,i}-cbar_k)-eta a_k.        (23)

Together with the fixed endpoint credit from (13)--(15), every such
continuous direction and EVERY integer tilt has total cap mass at least

    Gamma V_k+cbar_k-eta a_k
      >=Gamma V_k+Gamma a_k+(kappa_d/2)a_k.          (24)

By (5), the required budget is at most Gamma V_k+Gamma a_k. Thus (24)
has a strict positive mass margin. The Hausdorff approximation error
has only multiplied the O(a_k) translation; no additive approximation
loss independent of a_k has been charged to this small margin.

## 7. Every remaining direction and the vertical boundary mass

Put theta_i=n_i/|n_i| and choose rho=epsilon/sqrt(d)>0. A unit normal
u with |u-theta_i|<=rho is included in Section 6: multiplying its
cap by |n_i| gives e=|n_i|(u-theta_i), of norm at most epsilon.
The integer tilt is multiplied by the same positive factor and remains
unrestricted. Constants in the affine functional cancel from the cuts.

For T at its centroid, the equality directions in classical Grunbaum
are exactly theta_0,...,theta_d. A simplex pyramid apex is a vertex,
and the other d vertices determine its opposite base facet. On the
compact complement of the open rho-neighborhoods, its normalized cap
fraction therefore exceeds Gamma by a fixed positive gap G. If this
complement is empty there is nothing to prove outside the neighborhoods.

Uniform cap-volume convergence under B_k->T and y_k->g gives at least
V_k(Gamma+G/2) from B_k alone in every direction in this complement,
for all sufficiently large k. This exceeds Gamma(V_k+a_k), since
a_k/V_k->0. Cap convergence here follows directly from null limiting
hyperplane boundaries and compactness of the unit sphere; it concerns
volume, not the section-density assertion (18).

A purely integer through-(0,y_k) cap is z>=0 or z<=0 and contains
the WHOLE middle fiber, including its boundary mass. Its mass is W_k+V_k
or a_k+V_k and is no smaller than V_k. For all large k, (5) and
Gamma<1/2 give V_k>Gamma(a_k+V_k+W_k)/2. These vertical caps are thus
also covered, without incorrectly discarding their middle-fiber trace.

Finally every containing halfspace includes its parallel through-point
halfspace. Sections 6 and 7 prove (1) at (0,y_k) for all large k, a
contradiction to the failure sequence. Hence a positive rho_d exists.

## 8. What this does and does not reduce

This proves a boundary exclusion for arbitrary three full-dimensional
fibers whenever one endpoint has sufficiently small volume relative to
the middle. Unequal large volumes are included: the heavy-fiber case
settles them unless their discrepancy is smaller than a.

The compactness constant is not computed. The argument does not replace
an arbitrary extracted maximizer by simplex fibers of equal mass, and
does not assert that independently altering a nonsimplex fiber preserves
its sampled Minkowski inclusions. Instead it proves that an actual
failing sequence in this specific small-endpoint regime would converge
to simplices and would then admit an all-cap point repair with a positive
first-order budget. No ordinary maximum-depth statement is substituted
for a theorem about the true mixed centroid.

There is no claim here for arbitrary endpoint volume ratios, more than
three positive integer fibers, additional integer coordinates, or
intrinsic degeneracies. Those are material restrictions on this result.
